My preference is barbells, as they are what you need for the four big lifts: squat, deadlift, bench, and overhead press. I'll always take a free-weight over a machine. With a machine, you never know actually how much weight you're really moving and you have to move in the geometry the machine is designed for.

Barbells and dumbbells use more muscles than machines and as a result you will be weaker in comparison. Its also much harder to over train or damage anything with dumbbells and barbells.

As echoed below Barbells should be the core of your training followed by dumbbells and use machines for isolation as the smaller work groups.

Every single program worth a damn from anyone that has every made real progress in any sport follows this system.

TL;DR: Barbells be best, bro.

I'm unoriginal in that I structure my training around barbell movements first then use some dumbbells and (less) machines for assistance work.

Machines are kings of two things: Isolation work and immediate safety. Machines allow the lifter to focus his or her effort on a single joint movement in a much more precise fashion than free-weights. Similarly, the reduced freedom of movement and enhanced stability of the motion allows more weight for mimicking compound movements (i.e. OP's example of the bench machine). Often this is due to a combination of instinctively recruiting any muscle that helps complete the guided motion and stabilizers being too weak for the free-weight motion. To worsen the situation, ingraining the incorrect motion then makes the stabilizers more necessary for the free-weight motion. However, for the uninitiated, machines do substantially reduce the risk of being crushed by the weight should the lifter lose control.

Dumbbells offer moderate safety and can be used for isolation work, but they also can be used to bring additional stress to the stabilizers. Their safety comes from the fact that it is easier for the lifter to direct a drop away from himself or herself with dumbbells than larger weights. The single hand-held nature of the dumbbell also allows greater range of motion. With a little creativity and a supporting surface, many isolation movements can reduce the reliance on stabilizers. Conversely, compound movements would reduce supporting surfaces and decrease stability. Of course, this allows for greater use of the stabilizers, but it comes at a cost of reduced stress to the prime movers since the weight is reduced in order to maintain control.

Barbells offer the least safety but the greatest potential for strength gains. The reduction in safety results purely from the inability of the user to dodge the weight on a bad lift. To this end, new lifters must learn how to set-up, execute, and fail properly for barbell training. However, when properly executed, the barbell offers the most useful strength gains when compared to dumbbells and weights. For upper body work, this results from a reduction in the usage of stabilizers as compared to dumbbells while still requiring strict form control. Unlike dumbbells, the distance between the hands cannot appreciably change during the lift, so tiny corrections keeping the weight under control in directions parallel to the barbell don't hinder the motion. Importantly, the restriction of hand placement truly excels at teaching coordination between the left and right sides of the lifter. This teaches the lifter how to apply maximal strength from each side of the body simultaneously, which then translates to life when the training consists of functional movement archetypes. For lower body work, it more related to the difficultly loading sufficiently heavy weight with dumbbells. Most gyms don't over many dumbbells over 100 lbs, whereas trained squat/deadlift to body weight ratios are commonly around 1.5/2:1 for intermediate lifters.

In general, for most exercises use barbells, for some use dumbells. Avoid machines. The ideal method depends on your goals and the exercise, but any exercise is much better than no exercise.

Rationale:

  • Dumbells develop more secondary muscles than barbells, which exercises more the secondary muscles than machines. I say more, because all will build stabilizers to a degree, but machines are often considered to not build them enough. However, for this same reason, if you want to isolate a muscle, a machine might be the best solution, maybe because you are targeting that specific muscle for hypertrophy, or because you're injured and you want to avoid exercising the other muscles.
  • Machines are more forgiving to mistakes than barbells and dumbells.
  • Machines are easier to load with weight, and position, than barbells. Barbells are easier to load with weight, and position, than dumbells; typically dumbells have their 'plates' wielded, so you need to switch the entire dumbell, instead just switching a few plates.
  • Dumbells, barbells, and machines build different neurological patterns. You're more likely to use both hands in a movement, so barbells typically are closest to reality.

Feeling that you don't engage your pecs is not a sign that the exercise isn't working. If you maintain good form, and you're progressing, with your muscles getting bigger, doing more reps, more sets, and lifting more weight, you're doing it right.
